la:adj:ceterus.html:
cētĕrus (caet-), a, um (the
nom. sing. masc. not in use; the sing., in gen., rare; in Cic. perh. only three times), adj.
pronom. stem ki, and compar. ending; cf. ἕτερος
, the other, that which exists besides, can be added to what is already named of a like kind with it; the other part (while reliquus is that which yet remains of an object, the rest; e. g. stipendium pendere et cetera indigna pati,and endured other indignities of the kind,. On the other hand: jam vero reliqua—not cetera —quarta pars mundi ea et ipsa totā naturā fervida est, et ceteris naturis omnibus salutarem impertit et vitalem calorem,; cf. Hand, Turs. II. p. 33; Doed. Syn. 1, p. 83. Still these ideas, esp. after the Aug. per., are often confounded, and the Engl., the remainder, the rest, and the adverb. phrase for the rest, etc., can be used interchangeably for both words).
Sing.
Masc.: si vestem et ceterum ornatum muliebrem pretii majoris habeat, (also in ); : laeta et imperatori ceteroque exercitui,: vestitu calciatuque et cetero habitu,: illos milites subduxit, exercitum ceterum servavit, Cato ap. : cohortes veteranas in fronte, post eas ceterum exercitum in subsidiis locat,: a cetero exercitu,; ; : de cetero numero candidatorum,.—
Fem.: cetera jurisdictio,: vita,: aetas,: nox,: silva,: turba,; 12, 286; : classis,: deprecatio,; : inter ceteram planitiem mons,: Graeciam,: aciem,: multitudinem,: (super) turbam,: manum procerum,: pro ceterā ejus audaciā atque amentiā,: pluviā (aquā) utebantur,: ceterā (ex) copiā militum,; : ceterā (pro) reverentiā,: ceterā (cum) turbā,—
Neutr.: cum a pecu cetero absunt,: non abhorret a cetero scelere,; : cetero (e) genere hominum,: quanto violentior cetero mari Oceanus,—Subst.: cētĕ-rum, i, n., the rest: elocuta sum convivas, ceterum cura tu,: ceterum omne incensum est,; so, de cetero,as for the rest,; ; and in ceterum,for the rest, for the future,.—
Plur., the rest, the others (freq. in all periods and species of composition): de reliquis nihil melius ipso est: ceteri et cetera ejus modi, ut, etc.,: multae sunt insidiae bonis nosti cetera,; : cetera de genere hoc, adeo sunt multa, etc.,; : ut omittam cetera,: ibi Amineum... Lucanum serito, ceterae vites in quemvis agrum conveniunt,: quam fortunatus ceteris sim rebus, absque una hac foret,: nam ceteri fere, qui artem orandi litteris tradiderunt, ita sunt exorsi, quasi, etc., Quint. prooem. § 4; : ceterae partes loquentem adjuvant, hae ipsae loquuntur,: sane ceterarum rerum pater familias et prudens et attentus, unā in re paulo minus consideratus,: hanc inter ceteras vocem,: de justitiā, fortitudine, temperantiā ceterisque similibus, id. prooem. § 12; 3, 5, 5; 2, 4, 38: ego ceteris laetus, hoc uno torqueor,.—
Et cetera ceteraque or cetera, and so forth, καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς, when one refers to a well-known object with only a few words, or mentions only a few from a great number of objects, : ut illud Scipionis, Agas asellum et cetera,; ; ; ; : et similiter cetera,: vina ceteraque,; : solem, lunam, mare, cetera,: fundum, aedes, parietem, supellectilem, penus, cetera,. 27.—
Hence, the advv.,
cē-tĕrum (orig. acc. respectiv.), lit. that which relates to the other, the rest (besides what has been mentioned).
For the rest, in other respects, otherwise (in good prose): nihil, nisi ut ametis impero: Ceterum quantum lubet me poscitote aurum, ego dabo,: tu aurum rogato: ceterum (for the rest, in respect to the rest) verbum sat est, : precator, qui mihi sic oret: nunc amitte quaeso hunc; ceterum Posthac si quicquam, nil precor,: ego me in Cumano et Pompeiano, praeterquam quod sine te, ceterum satis commode oblectabam, (14), 1: foedera alia aliis legibus, ceterum eodem modo omnia fiunt,; cf. ; ; ; .—Rarely after the verb: argentum accepi; nil curavi ceterum,: numquid me vis ceterum? .—
= alioquin, introducing a conclusion contrary to fact (mostly post-class.), otherwise, else, in the opposite event, = Gr. ἄλλως: non enim cogitaras; ceterum Idem hoc melius invenisses,: ita et anima... solam vim ejus exprimere non valuit,... ceterum non esset anima, sed spiritus,; ; —
In passing to another thought, besides, for the rest; very freq. (esp. in the histt.; usu. placed at the beginning of a new clause; only in the comic poets in the middle): Filium tuom te meliust repetere, Ceterum uxorem abduce ex aedibus,; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; : dehinc ceterum valete,; cf. . —
With a restricting force, commonly contrasted with quidem or a neg. phrase; often to be translated by but, yet, notwithstanding, still, on the other hand (esp. freq. since the Aug. per.): cum haud cuiquam in dubio esset, bellum ab Tarquiniis imminere, id quidem spe omnium serius fuit: ceterum, id quod non timebant, per dolum ac proditionem prope libertas amissa est,; ; ; ; ; ; : eos multum laboris suscipere, ceterum ex omnibus maxume tutos esse,: avidus potentiae, honoris, divitiarum, ceterum vitia sua callide occultans,; 52, 1; 83, 1; : eo rem se vetustate oblitteratam, ceterum suae memoriae infixam adferre,: id quamquam, nihil portendentibus diis, ceterum neglegentia humana acciderat, tamen, etc.,; ; Weissenb. ad loc.: ut quisquis factus est princeps, extemplo fama ejus, incertum bona an mala, ceterum aeterna est,: pauca repetundarum crimina, ceterum magicas superstitiones objectabat,; cf. .—
cē-tĕra (properly acc. plur.), = τἆλλα, τὰ λοιπά, as for the rest, otherwise; with adjj., and (in poets) with verbs (not found in Cic. or Quint.).
With adj.: Bocchus praeter nomen cetera ignarus populi Romani,: hastile cetera teres praeterquam ad extremum,: excepto quod non simul esses, cetera laetus, (cf. the passage cited under ceterum, II. A. 1. fin., (14), 1): cetera Graius, (so prob. also , where others read ad cetera): virum cetera egregium secuta,: vir cetera sanctissimus, Ruhnk.; ; ; ; .—
With verbs: cetera, quos peperisti, ne cures, Enn. ap. : quiescas cetera,: cetera parce, puer, bello,; cf. : cetera non latet hostis,; .—
cētĕrō, peculiar to the Nat. Hist. of Pliny, for the rest, in other respects, otherwise: cetero viri quam feminae majus,; so ; ; ; 10, 1, 1, § 1 al.: est et alia iritis cetero similis, at praedura,.— Of time: palumbes incubat femina post meridiana in matutinum, cetero mas,.

la:adj:certus.html:
certus, a, um
orig. P. a. from cerno; hence
, adj.,
determined, resolved, fixed, settled, purposed: non dubius.
(Acc. to cerno, II. D.) Certum est (mihi), it is determined, it is my (thy, his, etc.) decision, resolution, will, I am resolved, I mean, etc. (mostly ante-class.; most freq. in Plaut.); with inf.: quorum virtuti belli Fortuna pepercit, Eorundem me libertati parcere certum est, Enn. ap. (Ann. v. 206 Vahl.): certum'st hominem eludere,: tibi credere,; cf. ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; : certum est deliberatumque, quae ad causam pertinere arbitror, omnia dicere, : certum atque decretum est non dare signum,: certum est igni circumdare muros,.—Certum'st mihi with inf., ; ; ; ; ; ; ; —Without inf., esp. parenthet., with expression of purpose by a fut. tense: certum est, malam rem potius quaeram cum lucro,: certum est, jam dicam patri,: certum est, ibo ad medicum,: An. Certumn' est tibi? Ly. Certum, ; cf. .—With pron. or subst.: Ar. Certumne'st tibi istuc? He. Non moriri certius, ; so further with istuc,; : mihi autem abjurare certius est quam dependere,: ad eum senem oppugnare certum est consilium,: quae nunc sunt certa ei consilia, etc.,: certa res hanc est objurgare,; so ; ; ; .—
(From the time of the Aug. poets.) Transf. to the person who is determined upon something, determined, resolved, bent.
With inf.: certa mori, (cf. : decrevitque mori): certi non cedere,: certa sequi,.—
With gen. (cf. Ramsh. Gr. p. 323; Zumpt, Gr. § 437, n. 1; A. and S. § 213, R. 1): certus eundi,; : desciscendi,: relinquendae vitae,: necis,: fugae,: destinationis,: sceleris,: consilii,.—
With an: nec sat certa an cederet armis,.—
An epithet of all those objects whose existence or reality is fixed, determined (hence in connection with definitus, ; with praefinitus,), or in respect to which there can be no doubt (hence opp. dubius, ; ; ).
Object.
Of things whose external qualities, number, etc., are invariable, established, settled, fixed, particular, specified, etc. (class.): Arboribus primum certis gravis umbra tributa,: fruges, bacae,: jam ad certas res conficiendas certos homines delectos ac descriptos habebat,: concilium in diem certam indicere,; so with dies,a fixed term,; ; ; ; ; cf.: certis diebus,: quaerere ab judicibus cur in certa verba jurent, cur certo tempore conveniant, certo discedant,; cf. : certum praefinitumque tempus,; and: certum statumque vectigal,: pecunia (opp. arbitraria), v. arbitrarius: finis aerumnarum,; cf. ; ; ; : locus,: numerus,: signum,fixed, agreed upon,: naves,fixed in number and quality,: pecuniae imperabantur,fin.: conviva,i. e. a daily, constant guest, Schmid: ecquem tu illo certiorem nebulonem,.—
But sometimes indef., like quidam, and our certain, of things, the certainty of whose existence is given, but whose nature is not more definitely designated, or comes not into consideration (cf. aliquis): Cephaloedi mensis est certus, quo mense sacerdotem maximum creari oporteat,: habet certos sui studiosos,: (hunc) certis rebus imperatis regnare jussit,: certi homines ad eam rem periti,: res a certis hominibus corrupta,; ; ; ; ; .—Hence in Quint. several times in connection with quidam and aliquis: ad certas quasdam dicendi leges alligati,; so ; ; ; ; ; : aliquos compositionis certos pedes,; so and subst.: in his certos aliquos docebit,.—
Trop., of things whose internal moral qualities are established, fixed, can be relied upon, sure, unerring, to be depended upon, true, faithful,

etc. (so most freq. in all periods and species of composition; syn.: firmus, confirmatus, exploratus, indubitatus, manifestus al.).

Of persons: amicus certus in re incertā cernitur, Enn. ap. ; cf.: tu ex amicis certis mi es certissimus,: certi homines, quibus dem litteras,; cf. ; ; ; ; : certus enim promisit Apollo, etc.,: auctor (mortis),; cf. : adversus hostem nec spe nec animo certiorem, i. e. firmiorem,: apud latera certos collocaverat, Sall. ap. (H. 1, 53 Dietsch); cf. : per litora certos dimittam,: certissimus auctor (Phoebus),.—
Of things: satis animo certo et confirmato,; cf. pectora,, and certior indoles, : promissa,: parata dicendi copia et certa,; : jus, et saep.: jactus (telorum),; cf. in this sense certa hasta,: sagitta,: fides segetis,: spes,: trames,: lar,: plana et certa,: certa et clara, Ruhnk.; so ; cf. .—Subst., with gen.: certa maris,.—
Subject., of that which is established by evidence, etc., placed beyond doubt, certain, sure, true, proved, established (class.; esp. freq. in neutr.): cum ad has suspitiones certissimae res accederent,; : incerta pro certis malebant,; cf.: incerta pro certis mutare,: postremo certior res,: certiora esse dicunt quam, etc.,; ; : So. Satin hoc certum'st? Ge. Certum: hisce oculis egomet vidi,: jam satis certumst virginem vitiatam esse?: cum certius tibi sit me esse Romae quam mihi te Athenis,: id parum certum est,: cum de altero intellectu certum est, de altero dubium,; cf. : non certum traditur, with interrog.-clause, : nec quicquam certi respondes mihi?: neque tanto spatio certi quid esset explorari poterat,: certum inveniri non potest ne ... an,: si quicquam humanorum certi est,: Ph. Civemne? Th. Arbitror: Certum non scimus,; cf. ; .—So, certum scire, to know for a certainty, ; ; : certum habere,to reckon certain,; ; ; ; : certum respondeo,: cognoscere, Auct. B. Alex. 53: comperire, Auct. B. Hisp. 22.—So also pro certo habere,; Matius ap. , A med.; ; : negare,: polliceri,: dicere aliquid,: ponere,: scire,: affirmare,; ; cf. Drak.: creditur,: coeperit esse,: certius cognoscere ex aliquo de aliquā re,.—Strengthened by comp.: quin nihil invenies magis hoc certo certius,; cf.: et hoc certo certius est et saepissime constitutum,: certo certius,; ; .—In Plaut. certum or certius facere alicui, to give certainty to one concerning any thing, make him certain, ; ; .—
Transf. to the person who is made certain in reference to a thing, certain, sure: certi sumus periisse omnia,: num quid nunc es certior?: posteritatis,i. e. of posthumous fame,: sententiae,: judicii,: certus de suā geniturā,: damnationis,: exitii,: spei,: matrimonii,: certi sumus, etc.,.—In class. prose mostly in the phrase certiorem facere aliquem (de aliquā re, alicujus rei, with a foll, acc. and inf., with a rel.-clause or absol.), to inform, apprise one of a thing: me certiorem face,: ut nos facias certiores,: uti se (sc. Caesarem) de his rebus certiorem faciant,: qui certiorem me sui consilii fecit,, a, 2: Caesarem certiorem faciunt, sese non facile ab oppidis vim hostium prohibere,: faciam te certiorem quid egerim,.— With subj. only: milites certiores facit, paulisper intermitterent proelium,—Pass.: quod crebro certior per me fias de omnibus rebus,; so ; : Caesar certior factus est, tres jam copiarum partes Helvetios id flumen transduxisse,; so ; 1, 41; 2, 1; ; : factus certior, quae res gererentur,: non consulibus certioribus factis,.—Also in posit., though rarely: fac me certum quid tibi est,; ; : lacrimae suorum Tam subitae matrem certam fecere ruinae,.— Hence, adv. in two forms.
certō, with certainty, certainly, surely, of a truth, in fact, really, object. and subject. (cf. supra, II. A. and B.); only in the comic poets, and sometimes (most. freq. in his epistt.) in Cic., while the adverbial form certe belongs to all periods and all species of composition. The difference between them is, perhaps, merely historical; but v.infra, certe, B. I. 2. init.
Object.: perii certo, haud arbitrario,; cf. : mihi certo nomen Sosia'st,; ; : nihil ita exspectare quasi certo futurum, (cf. the passage cited under certo, I. 1., from ).—
In affirm. answers: Me. Liberum ego te jussi abire? Mes. Certo, yes, certainly, ; so ; 2, 3, 38; ; .—
Subject.
In gen. (very rare): certo enim ego vocem hic loquentis modo mi audire visus sum,: ego rus abituram me esse certo decrevi,: Th. Quid aīs? Py. Atqui certo comperi, .—
Esp. in the formula of asseveration, certo scio, I certainly know, I am fully persuaded, beyond all doubt (class.): certo edepol scio, me vidisse, etc.,; ; ; ; ; : quod te moleste ferre certo scio,; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; : veniunt in mentem mihi permulta: vobis plura, certo scio, (cf. under certe, I. 2.).—
certē (class.; cf. supra, certo init.).
Affirming strongly, with certainty, certainly, undoubtedly, assuredly, surely, really.
Object.: certe edepol, tu me alienabis,: ego quidem ab hoc certe exorabo,: certe hercle,; cf. ; ; : quom is certe Renuntiarit,: certe captus est!: certe ut videamur cernere eum,: si enim scit, certe illud eveniet: sin certe eveniet, nulla fortuna est,; cf. : fuit certe id aequum et certe exspectatum est, etc.,: ea certe vera sunt,: M. Catoni certe licuit, etc.,: jam illa perfugia certe minime sunt audienda,: cum se certe decessurum videret,; : certe hinc Romanos olim fore ductores pollicitus,: o dea certe,a goddess surely,: postremo expellet certe vivacior heres,: placuit tibi, Delphice, certe, Dum, etc.,— Comp.: speculatores mittere, qui certius explorata referant,; : si reperire vocas amittere certius,; .—Sup., .—
In an answer of affirmation: estne ipsus an non est! Is est, Certe is est, is est profecto,; so ; ; ; ; ; and in confirmation of a preceding fact: venerat, ut opinor, haec res in judicium. Certe, certainly, surely, ; ; ; cf. ; .—
Subject., mostly in the phrase certe scio, I know to a certainty, I am sure (acc. to Klotz ad , certe scio = certum est me scire, I am fully convinced: certo scio = certum est quod scio, my knowledge is accurate, etc.): certe edepol scio, si aliud quicquam est quod credam aut certo sciam, etc.,: edepol certo scio,: scelestiorem me hac anu certe scio Vidisse numquam,; cf. : ex litteris certe scire potuistis,; : quod iste certe statuerat ac deliberaverat non adesse,.—
In affirm. answers: Ar. Ain' vero? Le. Certe, inquam, : Ch. Ain'tu? So. Certe, sic erit, .—
In a subjective supposition or presumption that a thing is so, certainly, surely, assuredly, doubtless, of course; Gr. ἴσως: ah nugas agis, Certe habes,; : si me tanti facis, quanti certe facis,; ; cf. ; ; . —
In interrog., ; .—
Affirming with restriction, yet surely, yet indeed, at least, notwithstanding (very freq. in prose and poetry, esp. after the class. per.).
Alone: si non ipsā re tibi istuc dolet, Simulare certe est hominis,: cingitur, certe expedit se,: ut homines mortem vel optare incipiant, vel certe timere desistant,: haec... sint falsa sane, invidiosa certe non sunt,: qui... ut non referat pedem, sistet certe,: res fortasse verae, certe graves,; cf. : consulatum unum certe plebis Romanae esse,: quos quoniam caeli nondum dignamur honore, Quas dedimus certe terras habitare sinamus, et saep.: quo quid sit beatius, mihi certe in mentem venire non potest,; so, ego certe,; : certe ego,; ; ; : mihi certe,: ipse certe,; ; .—
With other particles.
With tamen: illud certe tamen, quod jam amplexi sumus,; .—
With at: quod (consilium) si non fuerit prudens, at certe ab optima fide proficiscetur, Balb. et opp. ap. , A, 1; ; cf. at II. 3.—
With sed: non integrā re, sed certe minus infractā, quam, etc., Att. ap. ; cf. dub. B. and K. —
With quidem: ubi sit animus, certe quidem in te est,: quoniam volumus quidem certe senes fieri,; : certe quidem vos estis Romani, etc.,. (But quidem does not belong with certe in such passages as the foll.: hic quidem certe memorat, etc.,; v. quidem; cf. also aut and vel.)

la:verb:certioro.html:
certĭōro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
certior
, = certiorem facere,
to inform, apprise, show (only in jurid. Lat., and most freq. used by Ulpian), Gai 2, 190; ; fin.: certioratus,; .

senses: to register the citizens, perform the task of a censor
la:verb:censeo.html:
cēnseo (on the long
e, v. Corss. Ausspr. 1, p. 257 sq.), ui, cēnsum (late Lat. censitum, tit.; 11, 49 tit.; 11, 47, 4 al.; but not in Monum. Ancyr.; cf. Neue, Formenl. 2, 557), 2, v. a.
etym. dub.; often referred to root cas-, whence carmen, camoenus; but prob. from centum, orig. centere, to hundred or number the people; cf. Fischer, Gram. 1, p. 373
.
To tax, assess, rate, estimate.
In reference to the census (v. census).
Of the censor (v. censor).
Rarely act. with acc. of the persons or objects assessed or rated; but usu. pass., with subj. -nom.: censores populi aevitates, suboles, familias, pecuniasque censento,: census quom sum, juratori recte rationem dedi,: censor ad quojus censionem, id est arbitrium, populus censeretur, Müll.: census... indicat eum qui sit census se jam tum gessisse pro cive,: absentīs censere jubere, P. Scipio ap. : ne absens censeare. : sub lustrum censeri,: milia octoginta eo lustro civium censa dicuntur,: censa civium capita centum septendecim milia trecenta undeviginti,; ; ; : censebantur ejus aetatis lustrīs ducena quinquagena milia capitum,: cum capitum liberorum censa essent CLII. milia,: quid se vivere, quid in parte civium censeri, si... id obtinere universi non possint? Liv 7, 18, 5.—
With the amount at which the property was rated, in the acc.: or abl.: praesertim census equestrem Summam nummorum,being assessed with the estate necessary to a Roman knight,: primae classis homines quicentum et viginti quinque milia aeris ampliusve censi erant... Ceterarumque omnium classium qui minore summa aeris censebantur,—Hence, capite censi, those who were assessed ac cording to their ability to labor: qui nullo

aut perquam parvo aere censebantur capite censi vocabantur. Extremus autem census capite censorum aeris fuit trecentis septuaginta quinque, Jul. Paul. ap. ; ; ; ; ; ; and in the finite verb: omnia illius (i. e. sapientis) esse dicimus, cum... capite censebitur,. —

Absol. in gerund.: censendi, censendo, ad censendum = census agendi, censui agendo, etc.: haec frequentia quae convenit ludorum censendique causā (i.e. census agendi causā, for the sake of the census), : mentio inlata apud senatum est, rem operosam... suo proprio magistratu egere... cui arbitrium formulae censendi subiceretur,the scheme for taking the census,: quia is censendo finis factus est,: civīs Romanos ad censendum ex provinciis in Italiam revocarunt,: aetatem in censendo significare necesse est... aetas autem spectatur censendi tempore,.—
Censum censere = censum agere, only in the gerundial dat.: illud quaero, sintne illa praedia censui censendo, habeant jus civile,are they subject to the census,: censores... edixerunt, legem censui censendo dicturos esse ut, etc., that he would add a rule for the taking of the census, according to which, etc., : censui censendo agri proprie appellantur qui et emi et venire jure civili possunt, Paul. ex Müll.—
Of the assessment of the provinces under provincial officers (censores, and, under the later emperors, censitores).
Pass., with the territory as subject-nom.: quinto quoque anno Sicilia tota censetur; erat censa praetore Paeducaeo... quintus annus cum in te praetorem incidisset, censa denuo est,: omne territorium censeatur quoties, etc., (57), 4.—
The persons assessed as subject: ubi (coloni) censiti atque educati natique sunt, (47), 6: quos in locis eisdem censitos esse constabit, (47), 4.—With part. as attribute: rusticos censitosque servos vendi, (47), 7.—
To determine by the census: cum antea per singulos viros, per binas vero mulieres capitis norma sit censa, (47), 10: nisi forte privilegio aliquo materna origo censeatur,.—
Act. with acc.: vos terras vestras levari censitione vultis, ego vero etiam aërem vestrum censere vellem,.—
Of the person assessed, to value, make a statement of one's property in the census.
Act. with acc.: in quā tribu ista praedia censuisti?.—
Censeri, as dep. with acc.: census es praeterea numeratae pecuniae CXXX. Census es mancipia Amyntae... Cum te audisset servos suos esse censum, constabat inter omnes, si aliena censendo Decianus sua facere posset, etc.,; cf. ; v. B. 2. c.—
Hence, subst.: cēnsum, i, n.: quorum luxuries fortunata censa peperit, i.e. high estimates of property in the census, Cic. ap. (Fragm. vol. xi. p. 134 B. and K.).
Transf., of things and persons in gen., to value, estimate, rate.
By a figure directly referring to the Roman census: aequo mendicus atque ille opulentissimus Censetur censu ad Acheruntem mortuus, will be rated by an equal census, i.e. in the same class, without considering their property, : vos qui potestis ope vostrā censerier, referring to a part of the audience, you, who may be rated according to your intelligence, analog. to capite censi (v. I. A. 1. β), : nam argumentum hoc hic censebitur,will be rated, its census-class will be determined here,: id in quoque optimum esse debet cui nascitur, quo censetur, according to which he is rated, i.e. his worth is determined, .—And with two acc.: quintus Phosphorus, Junonia, immo Veneris stella censetur, is ranked as the fifth, App. de Mundo, p. 710.—
With direct reference to the census.
= aestimo, to estimate, weigh, value, appreciate.
With gen. of price: dic ergo quanti censes?.—
In the pass.: si censenda nobis atque aestimanda res sit, utrum tandem pluris aestimemus pecuniam Pyrrhi? etc., if we have to weighand estimate a thing, etc., : anule... In quo censendum nil nisi dantis amor,: interim autem facta sola censenda dicit atque in judicium vocanda,—
= honorari, celebrari, with de aliquo, = for the sake of somebody (in Ovid): pro quibus ut maneat, de quo censeris, amicus, Comprecor, etc.,the friend for the sake of whom you are celebrated, who is the cause of your renown,: hoc domui debes de quā censeris,.—
Censeri, dep., = to distinguish, with acc. only once or twice in Ovid (v. I. A. 3. β): hanc semper... Est inter comites Marcia censa suas,has always distinguished her,.—
Censeri aliquā re.
= to be appreciated, distinguished, celebrated for some quality, as if the quality were a standard determining the census, analog. to capite censeri (v. I. A. 1. β), very freq. in post-class. writings: Democritus cum divitiis censeri posset,when he might have been celebrated for his wealth,, ext. 4: Aristides quo totius Graeciae justitia censetur (quo = cujus justitiā),, ext. 3 med.: te custode matronalis stola censetur ( = tuā, i.e. pudicitiae, custodiā), the stola, etc., is appreciated for thy custody, prooem.: unā adhuc victoriā Carius Metius censebatur,: ut ipsi quoque qui egerunt non aliis magis orationibus censeantur,: non vitibus tantum censeri Chium, sed et operibus Anthermi filiorum, is celebrated not only for its grapes, but, etc., : et Galliae censentur hoc reditu,: quisquis paulo vetustior miles, hic te commilitone censetur,is distinguished for the fact that you were his fellow-soldier,: multiplici variāque doctrinā censebatur,: felix quae tali censetur munere tellus,: censetur Apona Livio suo tellus, = for the fact that Livy was born there, : hi duo longaevo censentur Nestore fundi,for the fact that Nestor used them,: nec laude virorum censeri contenta fuit (Iberia),: libri mei non aliā laude carius censentur, quam quod judicio vestro comprobantur,.—Hence,
= to be known by something (Appuleian): hoc nomine censebatur jam meus dominus,: nomen quo tu censeris aiebat,, p. 106: pro studio bibendi quo solo censetur, either known by, or distinguished for, : globorum caelestium supremum esse eum qui inerrabili meatu censetur,which is known by its unerring course,.— And,
As gram. t. t., to be marked by some peculiarity, according to which a word is classified: neque de armis et moeniis infitias eo quin figurā multitudinis perpetuā censeantur, that they are marked by the form of constant plurality, i. e. that they are pluralia tantum, ; ; .
Of transactions in and by the Senate, to judge (in the meanings II. and III. the passive voice is not in class. use, while in I. the passive voice is by far the most freq.).
To be of opinion, to propose, to vote, to move, referring to the votes of the senators when asked for their opinions (sententiam dicere).
With a (passive) inf.-clause, denoting what should be decreed by the Senate (esse usu. omitted): rex his ferme verbis patres consulebat... Dic, inquit ei, quid censes? tum ille Puro pioque duello quaerendas (res) censeo, I am of the opinion (I move, propose) that satisfaction should be sought, etc., ancient formula ap. : primum igitur acta Caesaris servanda censeo,: hoc autem tempore ita censeo decernendum,; 5, 6, 16; 5, 12, 31; 5, 12, 34; 5, 13, 36; 5, 14, 38; 5, 19, 53; 6, 1, 2; 9, 6, 14; 11, 15, 40; 12, 7, 17; 14, 1, 1; 14, 13, 35; cf. Regulus's advice in the Senate, being represented as a vote: captivos in senatu reddendos non censuit,; : quare ita ego censeo... de confessis more majorum supplicium sumendum,; ; : Appius imperio consulari rem agendam censebat,: ut multi (senatores) delendam urbem censerent,; ; ; 10, 12, 1; 34, 4, 20; 38, 54, 6: cum ejus diei senatus consulta aureis litteris figenda in curiā censuisset, : ut nonnulli dedendum eum hostibus censuerint,; so ; ; ; ; ; ; . Of the emperor's vote in the Senate: commutandam censuit vocem, et pro peregrinā nostratem requirendam,; so ; .—And with the copula expressed (very rare): qui censet eos... morte esse multandos,.—Sometimes referring to sententia as subject: sententia quae censebat reddenda bona (inst. of eorum qui censebant),.—Sometimes with oportere for the gerundial predic. inf.: quibusdam censentibus (eum) Romulum appellari oportere,.—With pres. inf., inst. of a gerundial: hac coronā civicā L. Gellius in senatu Ciceronem consulem donari a re publicā censuit, (cf. II. B. 1. b.).—If the opinion of the senator does not refer to the chief question, but to incidental points, the predic. inf. may have any form: eas leges quas M. Antonius tulisse dicitur omnes censeo per vim et contra auspicia latas, eisque legibus populum non teneri,: cum magna pars senatus... cum tyrannis bellum gerendum fuisse censerent... et urbem recipi, non capi, etc.,.—
With ut, and negatively, ut ne or ne, generally when the clause has an active predicate, but also with passives instead of the gerundial inf.-clause: de eā re ita censeo uti consules designati dent operam uti senatus Kal. Jan. tuto haberi possit,: censeo ut iis qui in exercitu Antonii sunt, ne sit ea res fraudi, si, etc.,: censebant omnes fere (senatores) ut in Italiā supplementum meis et Bibuli legionibus scriberetur,: Cn. Pompeius (in senatu) dixit, sese... censere ut ad senatūs auctoritatem populi quoque Romani beneficium erga me adjungeretur,: quas ob res ita censeo: eorum qui cum M. Antonio sunt, etc. ... iis fraudi ne sit quod cum M. Antonio fuerint,: Calidius, qui censebat ut Pompeius in suas provincias proficisceretur,: censuerunt quidam (senatores) ut Pannonicus, alii ut Invictus cognominaretur,: iterum censente ut Trebianis... concederetur (of the emperor's vote in the Senate),.—And an inf.-clause, with neu or ut: sed ita censeo: publicandas eorum pecunias, etc.: neu quis postea de his ad senatum referat, etc.,: qui partem bonorum publicandam, pars ut liberis relinqueretur, censuerat,.—
With a subj.-clause, without ut (rare in this connection; v. III. C. 3.): K. Fabius censuit... occuparent patres ipsi suum munus facere, captivum agrum plebi quam maxime aequaliter darent,.— And ironically with regard to incidental points: vereamini censeo ne... nimis aliquid severe statuisse videamini, I propose you should be afraid of having decreed too severe a punishment = of course, you will not be afraid, etc., : misereamini censeo—deliquere homines adulescentuli per ambitionem—atque etiam armatos dimittatis, I propose that you pity them, etc., or I advise you to be merciful, .—
Ellipt., with a gerundial clause understood: dic quid censes (i. e. decernendum),: quod ego meā sententiā censebam (i.e. decernendum), Cato ap. : senati decretum fit, sicut ille censuerat,: quas ob res ita censeo... senatui placere, etc. ( = ita decernendum censeo, etc.),; sq.; 11, 12, 29 sq.; 14, 14, 36 sq.—
= sententiam dicere, to tell, to express one's opinion in the Senate (post-class.).
Absol.: Priscus Helvidius .. contra studium ejus (sc. Vitellii) censuerat, had voted, or had expressed an opinion against his wishes, : cum parum sit, in senatu breviter censere, nisi, etc.,: sententias... prout libuisset perrogabat... ac si censendum magis quam adsentiendum esset,: igitur Cn. Piso, quo, inquit, loco censebis, Caesar? si primus, etc.,.—
With adjectives in the neuter, substantively used: nec quoquam reperto (in senatu) qui... referre aut censere aliquid auderet, who dared to express an opinion on any

thing, : per dissensionem diversa censentium,of the senators who expressed different opinions,.—

With interrog. or rel.-clause: deinde ageret senatorem et censeret quid corrigi aut mutari vellet,: cum censeat aliquis (in senatu) quod ex parte mihi placeat,.
Of the decrees or resolutions of the Senate, = decernere, placere, to resolve, decree.
With inf.-clause.
With gerund, without copula (v. II. A. 1.): eum, cujus supplicio senatus sollennes religiones expiandas saepe censuit,: eos senatus non censuit redimendos,; so ; : senatus Caelium ab republicā removendum censuit,: senatus censuit frequens coloniam Labicos deducendam,; : cum bello persequendos Tusculanos patres censuissent,; ; ; 7, 19, 7 et saep.—
With pres. inf. pass. or act., with the force of a gerundial: de bonis regiis quae reddi antea censuerant ( = reddenda),: munera mitti legatis ex binis milibus aeris censuerunt (i.e. patres),; so (v. 2. b.): eundem jus dicere Romae... patres censuerant,: cum senatus unum consulem, nominatimque Gnaeum Pompeium fieri censuisset,.—With both act. and pass. inf.: censuere patres, duas provincias Hispaniam rursus fieri... et Macedoniam Illyricumque eosdem... obtinere,.—With both pres. pass. and gerund. inff.: haec ita movere senatum, ut non expectanda comitia consuli censerent, sed dictatorem... dici,.— And with velle: senatus verbis nuntient, velle et censere eos ab armis discedere, etc.,.—
With ut or ne.
In the words of the Senate, according to formula: quod L. Opimius verba fecit de re publicā, de eā re ita censuerunt uti L. Opimius consul rem publicam defenderet, etc., ancient S. C. ap. : quod, etc., de eā re ita censuerunt ut M. Pomponius praetor animadverteret curaretque ut si, etc., S. C. ap. ; .—And with gerundial inf.-clause: quod C. Julius pontifex... de eā re ita censuerunt, uti M. Antonius consul hostiis majoribus... procuraret... Ibus uti procurasset satis habendum censuerunt, S. C. ap. .—
As related by the historians, etc.: quoniam senatus censuisset, uti quicunque Galliam provinciam obtineret... Aeduos defenderet,: patres censuerunt uti consules provincias inter se compararent,: senatus censuit ut domus ei... publicā impensā restitueretur,; so with reference to the civil law,quater.—With ne: senatum censuisse, ne quis illo anno genitus educaretur,.—And with inf -clause: filio regis Nicomedi ex eā summā munera dari censuerunt, et ut victimae... praeberentur,.—
With a subj.-clause (very rare): senatus consulto quo censeretur, darent operam consules, etc.,.—
With neutr. acc. pron. in place of a clause: cum vero id senatus frequens censuisset (sc. faciendum),: ite in suffragium, et quae patres censuerunt vos jubete,: quodcunque vos censueritis,: quodpatres censuissent,.—
With accusative of a noun, or a noun as passive subject, to decree or vote a thing (postclass.): nec tamen repertum nisi ut effigies principum, aras deum, templa et arcus aliaque solita... censuere,: aram Clementiae, aram Amicitiae, effigiesque... censuere,: cum censeretur clipeus auro et magnitudine insignis inter auctores eloquentiae (to be placed among, etc.), .—
With both acc. and dat.
The dat. = against: bellum Samnitibus et patres censuerunt et populus jussit,.—
The dat. = in behalf of: censentur Ostorio triumphi insignia,.—And with ut: sententiis eorum qui supplicationes et... vestem Principi triumphalem, utque ovans urbem iniret, effigiesque ejus... censuere,.
Transf.
Of the opinions and resolutions of other deliberating bodies, or of their members, to resolve, or to be of opinion.
With inf.-clause.
Gerundial: erant qui censerent de tertiā vigiliā in castra Cornelia recedendum (council of war),: erant sententiae quae conandum omnibus modis castraque Vari oppugnanda censerent,; so ; ; ; : pontifices, consules, patres conscripti mihi ... pecuniā publicā aedificandam domum censuerunt,: nunc surgendum censeo, I move we adjourn (in a literary meeting), : cum... pontifices solvendum religione populum censerent,: nunc has ruinas relinquendas non censerem (in an assembly of the people),: ego ita censeo, legatos extemplo Romam mittendos (in the Carthaginian Senate),: ante omnia Philippum et Macedonas in societatem belli... censeo deducendos esse (Hannibal in a council of war),; ; ; : cum septem judices cognovissent, duo censuerunt, reum exilio multandum, duo alii pecuniā, tres reliqui capite puniendum,.—And with oportere inst. of a gerundial clause (referring to duty): neque sine gravi causā eum locum quem ceperant, dimitti censuerant oportere,.—With opus esse ( = expediency): Parmenio furto, non proelio opus esse censebat,.—
With ordinary pres. inf.
In place of a gerundial: Antenor censet belli praecidere = praecidendam causam (in a council of war),.—
Denoting opinion about an existing state: Hasdrubal ultimam Hispaniae oram... ignaram adhuc Romanorum esse, eoque Carthaginiensibus satis fidam censebat,: Parmenio non alium locum proelio aptiorem esse censebat,.—
With ut or ne: censeo ut satis diu te putes requiesse et iter reliquum conficere pergas (in a literary meeting),: plerique censebant ut noctu iter facerent (council of war),: et nunc magnopere censere, ut unam anum ... triginta milibus talentum auri permutet (council of war),: censeout D. Claudius ex hac die deus fiat (council of the gods),: antiquos audio censuisse, ne (praenomina) cui ejusdem gentis patricio inderentur, resolved (family council), (cf. ).—
With subj.-clause: nunc quoque arcessas censeo omnes navalís terrestrīsque copias (Hannibal in council of war),: censeo relinquamus nebulonem hunc, eamus hinc protinus Jovi Optimo Maximo gratulatum (assembly of the people), Scipio Afric. ap. .—
With acc. neutr. of a pron. or adj. substantively used: ego pro sententiā meā hoc censeo: quandoquidem, etc.,: nec dubitavere quin vera censeret,that his opinion was correct,.—
Ellipt.: sententiis quarum pars deditionem, pars eruptionem censebat (i.e. faciendam),: ita uti censuerant Italici deditionem facit,; so .
Of the orders of persons in authority (cf. II. B.).
Of commanders, etc., by courtesy, inst. of velle, imperare, or a direct imperative sentence.
With gerundial inf. - clause: non tam imperavi quam censui sumptus legatis quam maxime ad legem Corneliam decernendos, I said, not strictly as an order, but as an opinion that, etc. (Cicero as proconsul), .—
With subj.-clause: arma quae ad me missuri eratis, iis censeo armetis milites quos vobiscum habetis, you had better, etc., Pomp. ap. , A, 4. —
Of an order by the people (rare; gen. populus jubet): ita id (foedus) ratum fore si populus censuisset (i. e. confirmandum esse),.—
Of the later emperors, in their ordinances (censemus = placet nobis, sancimus, imperamus, from the custom of the earlier emperors, who conveyed their commands in the form of an opinion in the senate; v. II. A. 1.).—With inf.clause, ut, ne, and subj.-clause: sex mensium spatium censemus debere servari, (47), 7: censemus ut, etc., (38), 13: censemus ne, etc., (45), 1: censemus vindicet, remaneat, ib. 11, 48 (47), 23: in commune jubes si quid censesve tenendum, Primus jussa subi,.
Of advice, given by one person to another (further development of III. A.).
Ante-class. formula: faciundum censeo = I advise, with ut-clause, with quid, sic, etc.: censeo faciundum ut quadringentos aliquos milites ad verrucam illam ire jubeas, etc., I advise you to order, etc., Cato ap. : ego Tiresiam... consulam, Quid faciundum censeat,consult Tiresias as to what he advises, for his advice,: consulam hanc rem amicos quid faciundum censeant,; : sic faciundum censeo: Da isti cistellam, etc.,: ego sic faciundum censeo: me honestiu'st Quam te, etc.,; : sane faciundum censeo,.—
With ordinary gerundial inf.-clauses: narrandum ego istuc militi censebo,I advise you to let the soldier know that,: exorando sumendam operam censeo,: quid nunc consili captandum censes?; ; : idem tibi censeo faciendum,: quos quidem tibi studiose et diligenter tractandos magno opere censeo,; .—Sometimes by aequum censere with an inf.-clause (in the comic poets): amicos consulam quo me modo Suspendere aequom censeant potissumum,: qui homo cum animo... depugnat suo, Utrum ita se esse mavelit ut eum animus aequom censeat, An ita potius ut parentes ... velint i. e. as his mind prompts him, ; cf. A. 3.).—Of an advice given to an adversary, with irony: cetera si qua putes te occultius facere posse... magnopere censeo desistas,I strongly advise you to give up that idea,: sed tu, Acci, consideres censeo diligenter, utrum censorum judicium grave esse velis an Egnatii,: postulant ut excipiantur haec inexplicabilia. Tribunum censeant: aliquem adeant: a me... numquam impetrabunt,: ibi quaeratis socios censeo, ubi Saguntina clades ignota est,: solvas censeo, Sexte, creditori,.—And in jest: Treviros vites censeo, audio capitalīs esse,: hi Plebei fuerunt, quos contemnas censeo... quā re ad patres censeo revertare,: vites censeo porticum Philippi: si te viderit Hercules, peristi,; so ; 12, 61, 7.—For ironical senatorial advice, by which the contrary is meant, v. ; , quoted II. A. 3.—
With an ut-clause (with monere; very rare): illud tamen vel tu me monuisse vel censuisse puta... ut tu quoque animum inducas, etc.,.—
With a clause understood: quo me vortam nescio: Pa. Si deos salutas, dextrovorsum censeo (i.e. id facias or faciundum censeo), : quo redeam? Pe. Equidem ad phrygionem censeo (i. e. redeas), : quid nunc censes, Chrysale? (i. e. faciundum),: ita faciam ut frater censuit,: tibi igitur hoc censeo (i. e. faciendum): latendum tantisper ibidem, etc.,: tu

potes Kalendis spectare gladiatores, et ita censeo, : quid censes igitur? Ecquidnam est tui consilii ad? etc.,: quid igitur censet (sapientia)? What is wisdom's advice? : scribi quid placeat, quid censeas,: ibitur igitur, et ita quidem ut censes,: disce, docendus adhuc, quae censet amiculus,.

Of opinions and views on general questions, to be of opinion, think, believe, hold (cf.: statuo, existimo, puto, aio, dico; freq. in class. prose; very rare in post-class. writers except Gellius; never with ut, ne, or subj.-clause).
With inf.-clause: Plato mundum esse factum censet a deo sempiternum,: Cyrenaici non omni malo aegritudinem effici censent, sed insperato,: (Hieronymus) censet summum bonum esse sine ullā molestiā vivere,: Aristoteles eos qui valetudinis causā furerent, censebat habere aliquid in animis praesagiens,: Pythagoras censuit animum esse per naturam rerum omnem intentum et commeantem,; so ; ; ; ; ; 3, 21, 70; 4, 7, 17; 5, 7, 17; ; ; ; 1, 13, 35 and 37; 1, 43, 120; 1, 44, 121; 2, 22, 57; 2, 16, 44; ; ; ; ; ; 1, 45, 108; 3, 5, 11; 3, 22, 52; 4, 7, 14; : Plato in civitate communīs esse mulieres censuit,; ; ; 19, 12, 6.—If the opinion refers to what should be observed, oportere or debere is used, or a gerundial predicate with esse (so in Cic., but in , without esse): oportere delubra esse in urbibus censeo,: M. Varro aeditumum dici oportere censet,; ; so with debere,; : Cyrenaici... virtutem censuerunt ob eam rem esse laudandam,: (Ennius) non censet lugendam esse mortem quam immortalitas consequatur,.—
An inf.-clause understood: (dissensio est), a quibus temporibus scribendi capiatur initium. Ego enim ab ultimis censeo (i. e. exordiendum esse),: si, Mimnermus uti censet, sine amore jocisque Nil est jucundum,: sic enim censuit,.—
With neutr. acc. of a pron.: hoc amplius censeo, in addition to the opinions mentioned I hold, etc., : nullo (medico) idem censente,.—
With a rel.-clause: Aesopus quae utilia... erant, non severe neque imperiose praecepit et censuit,he imparted his teachings and views,.—
Absol.: non adligo me ad unum aliquem ex Stoicis proceribus. Est et mihi censendi jus,the right to impart my opinions,.
In gen., = arbitror, puto, existimo, judico (cf.: idem enim valet censere et arbitrari, Varr. ap. : censere nunc significat putare, nunc suadere, nunc decernere, Paul. ex Müll.).
To judge, think, believe, suppose (freq. in ante-class. writings; very rare in Cic. except in the particular meanings, a.—ironically—and d.; always with inf.-clause expressed or understood).
In gen.: atque ego censui abs te posse hoc me impetrare,: satis jam delusam censeo: rem, ut est, nunc eloquamur,: nam si honeste censeam te facere posse, suadeam,: neque ego hac noctem longiorem me vidisse censeo,: saluti quod tibi esse censeo,; so ; ; ; ; sq.; ; ; ; ; ; ; : aut domino, cujum id censebis esse, reddes, Cincius, Re Mil. l. iii., de ap. : eo namque omnem belli molem inclinaturam censebant (consules),: nec facturum aequa Samnitium populum censebant, si... oppugnarent,: quaeso ut ea quae dicam non a militibus imperatori dicta censeas,: at illa purgare se, quod quae utilia esse censebat ... suasisset,: Alexander, tam memorabili victoriā laetus, quā sibi Orientis fines apertos esse censebat, ; so .—
With reference to an erroneous opinion, to imagine, suppose, falsely believe: censebam me effugisse a vitā maritumā Ne navigarem, etc.,: omnes eum (sc. Jovem) esse (Amphitruonem) censent servi,: jam hic ero, quom illic censebis esse me,: ardere censui aedes,: ego hunc censebam esse te,; so ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; et saep.: censuit se regem Porsenam occidere, Cass. Hem. ap. : non ipsa saxa magis sensu omni vacabant quam ille... cui se hic cruciatum censet optare,.—And ironically: nisi forte Diagoram aut Theodorum... censes superstitiosos fuisse,: nisi forte etiam illi Semproniano senatus consulto me censes adfuisse, qui ne Romae quidem fui,: neminem me fortiorem esse censebam,.—
Referring to what should take place.
With gerundial inf.-clause: navis praedatoria, Abs quā cavendum nobis sane censeo,: soli gerundum censeo morem,: neque vendundam censeo Quae libera est,; so ; ; ; : ceterum ei qui consilium adferret opem quoque in eam rem adferendam censebant esse,.—
With oportere, debere, or an ordinary inf.-clause: solam illi me soli censeo esse oportere obedientem,: quibus declaraveram, quo te animo censerem esse oportere, et quid tibi faciendum arbitrarer,: rursus interrogatus quid ipse victorem statuere debere censeret,: impudens postulatio visa est, censere... ipsos id (bellum) advertere in se, agrosque suos pro alienis populandos obicere, to entertain the idea that they should direct that war against themselves and their own lands, etc., : munere eum fungi prioris censet amici = eum fungi oportere,: quae nos quoque sustinere censebat,.—
By aequum censere with ordinary inf.clause, expressed or understood, either = it is fair (right) to do something, or something ought or should be done (so very freq. in the comic poets and Livy; rare in other writers): non ego istunc me potius quam te metuere aequom censeo, I do not think it right to fear him, etc., : quid me aequom censes pro illā tibi dare? What do you think I should give as a fair price? etc., : meum animum tibi servitutem servire aequom censui, I thought it my duty that my mind should, etc., : ecquis est tandem qui vestrorum... aequom censeat poenas dare ob eam rem quod arguatur male facere voluisse? Cato ap. : quis aequum censeret... receptos in fidem non defendi?; so ; ; .—And without emphasis upon the idea of fairness or right: si sunt ita ut ego aequom censeo,as I think they ought to be,; so ; ; ; ; ; ; : qui aequom esse censeant, nos jam a pueris ilico nasci senes,who believe that we should be born as old men right from childhood,; so ; : qui aequom censeant rem perniciosam utili praeponi,: (tribuni) intercedebant; senatum quaerere de pecuniā non relatā in publicum... aequum censebant,: cives civibus parcere aequum censebat,.—
Very freq., esp. in Cic., when a question, rhetorical or real, is addressed to a second person, often referring to erroneous opinions: an fores censebas nobis publicitus praeberier?: clanculum istaec te flagitia facere censebas potesse?: hicine nos habitare censes?: omnes cinaedos esse censes, tu quia es?; so ; ; ; . 82; ; ; ; ; : continuo dari Tibi verba censes? ; so ; 4, 4, 55; ; ; ; : adeone me delirare censes ut ista esse credam?: nam cum in Graeco sermone haec... non videbantur, quid censes in Latino fore?: quid igitur censes? Apim illum nonne deum videri Aegyptiis?: quis haec neget esse utilia? quem censes?: an censes me tantos labores... suscepturum fuisse, si, etc.,: an vos Hirtium pacem velle censetis?; so ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; 11, 1, 3; 11, 5, 10; 12, 3, 7; 12, 6, 13; 12, 8, 21; 12, 9, 22; 13, 2, 4; 14, 4, 10; : quid censes munera terrae?... quo spectanda modo, quo sensu credis et ore? sqq.; so ; (with obj.inf.).—With conditional period inst. of an inf.-clause: num censes faceret, filium nisi sciret eadem haec velle,.— Sometimes censemus? is used in the same way as censes?; ; .—
With an inf.clause understood: itane tu censes? Pa. Quid ego ni ita censeam? : quid ergo censes? Tr. Quod rogas, Censeo, : quid illum censes? (i. e. eo loco facere?) : quid illas censes? (i. e. posse dicere),; so ; ; .—So, very freq. in the comic poets, censeo, absol., as an approving answer; also sic censeo, istuc censeo, ita censeo (Cic.) to be variously rendered: ego divinam rem intus faciam... So. Censeo, that will be right! : auscultemus quid agat: Ph. Sane censeo, so we will, indeed, : quid si recenti re aedis pultem? Ad. Censeo, do so! : quin eloquamur? Ag. Censeo, hercle, patrue, : patri etiam gratulabor? Tr. Censeo, I think so (and after answering several questions with censeo): etiamne complectar ejus patrem? Tr. Non censeo. Pl. Nunc non censet quom volo, sqq.; ; ; ; ; ; : male habeas! Mu. Sic censeo, : aliquem arripiamus, etc.: Ly. Hem, istuc censeo, (cf.: prorsus ita censeo, referring to general questions, as in D.,); once similarly censeas: Quid gravare? censeas!Say yes,.—
To resolve, as a merely mental act, with gerundial inf.-clause (rare; cf. II. B.): quibus rebus cognitis, Caesar maturandum sibi censuit, resolved to hasten, lit., thought he must hasten ( = statuit, existimavit), : censuimus igitur amplius quaerendum,.—
To consider, i. e. after carefully weighing the circumstances, with inf.-clause (rare): sed cum censerem... me et periculum vitare posse, et temperatius dicere... ea causa mihi in Asiam proficiscendi fuit,.—
= pu tare, habere, judicare, to consider as, to hold, with two acc., or inf.-clause.
With double acc.: quom dispicias tristem, frugi censeas (i.e. eum),you would consider him thrifty,. 32: auxilio vos dignos censet senatus,considers you worthy of help,: has... indagines cuppediarum majore detestatione dignas censebimus si, etc.,: cum Priscum nobilitas hostem patriae censuisset, judged, declared him the enemy, etc., .—
In the pass. with nom. and inf., = haberi (in Manil. and Gell.): praeter illas unam et viginti (comoedias) quae consensu omnium Plauti esse censebantur,: quae terrenā censentur sidera sorte (i. e. esse),are considered as being of the terrestrial kind,; so ; ; ; 3, 96; so, sub aliquo censeri, to be considered as being under one's influence, ; ; cf. (with per).—
To wish, with subj.-clause or ne (in App.): de comā pretiosi velleris floccum mihi confestim adferas censeo,.

p. 117: censeo ne ulla cura os percolat,.

la:verb:cedo.gloss: to go, move, proceed, go along, move along
senses: to go, move, proceed, go along, move along
to result, turn out, happen, yield
to withdraw, depart, retire, go away from, yield
to pass, elapse (in the 3rd person, with time as subject)
to cede, give in or yield (to), step aside (for), give way (to)
to concede, give up, allow, permit something to someone, grant, surrender, yield
to fall (to) (as a possession); accrue or come (to)
to become, turn into, be or become the equivalent of
la:verb:cedo.html:
cēdo, cessi, cessum, 3, v. n. and a.
[perh. for cecado, redupl. from cado], to go, i. e. to be in motion, move, walk, go along.
In gen.
Lit. (rare, and only poet.: for which, in the common lang., incedo); candidatus cedit hic mastigia,: non prorsus, verum transvorsus cedit, quasi cancer,; cf. ; .—More freq.,
Trop.
Like ire, to have some result, to eventuate, happen, result, turn out, to work; and, acc. to its connection, to turn out well or ill, to succeed or fail: gesta quae prospere ei cesserunt,; ; : cetera secundum eventum proelii cessura,; ; : bene,; ; : optime,: male,; and: male alicui,; ; cf. ; : utcumque cesserit,; cf. ; : parum,: opinione tardius,: pro bono,: in vanum (labor),. —
Cedere pro aliquā re, to be equivalent to, to go for something, to be the price of: oves, quae non peperint, binae pro singulis in fructu cedent,; ; ; .—
In partic.
In respect to the terminus a quo.
To go from somewhere, to remove, withdraw, go away from, depart, retire (freq. and class.): cedunt de caelo corpora avium, Vahl.: quia postremus cedis,: ego cedam atque abibo,: cedens carinā,; cf. : quoquam,: aliquo sucus de corpore cessit,: coma de vertice,: e toto corpore anima,: ex ingratā civitate,: e patriā,: patriā,: Italiā,; ; —
Milit. t. t.: de oppidis,to abandon, go away from,: loco,to yield, give up his post,; ; ; et saep.: ex loco,: ex acie,.—
In commercial lang. t. t.: foro, to withdraw from themarket, i. e. to give up business, be insolvent, stop payment, ; ; .—So also,
Bonis or possessionibus (alicui), to give up or cede one's property or interest (in favor of a person): alicui hortorum possessione,; so ; cf. ; ; ; .— Hence of debtors, to make over their property instead of payment; cf. , tit. de cessione bonorum.—
Pregn. (cf. abeo, II.), to pass away, disappear; and specif.,
Of men, to die: vitā,; : e vita,; ; cf. senatu,to withdraw from,; .—
Of time, to pass away, vanish: horae quidem cedunt et dies et menses et anni,. —
Of other things: pudor ex pectore cessit, Lucil. ap. : memoriā, (for which: excedere memoriā,; and: excedere e memoriā,): non Turno fiducia cessit,: cedant curaeque metusque, et saep.; cf. cesso.—
Trop.: cedere alicui or absol., to yield to one (to his superiority), to give the preference or precedence, give place to, submit to (class.; esp. freq. in the histt., of the weaker party, withdrawing, fleeing from).
To yield to, give place to: quācumque movemur, (aër) videtur quasi locum dare et cedere,: cedebat victa potestas,: ubi vinci necesse est, expedit cedere,; ; ; cf. : Viriatho exercitus nostri imperatoresque cesserunt,; ; ; ; ; ; et saep.: Pelides cedere nescius,: di, quibus ensis et ignis Cesserunt,i. e. who remained unhurt in the destruction of Troy,: eidem tempori, ejusdem furori, eisdem consulibus, eisdem minis, insidiis, periculis,; so, fortunae,: invidiae ingratorum civium,: majorum natu auctoritati,: nocti,, and 3, 60, 7; 4, 55, 5; cf. : loco iniquo, non hosti cessum,: oneri,: vincentibus vitiis,: malis, et saep.—
To yield to in rank, distinction, etc., i. e. to be inferior to: cum tibi aetas nostra jam cederet, fascesque summitteret,: nullā aliā re nisi immortalitate cedens caelestibus,: neque multum cedebant virtute nostris,; : Picenis cedunt pomis Tiburtia suco; Nam facie praestant,; so, anseribus (candore),: laudibus lanificae artis,; 5, 529: cum in re nullā Agesilao cederet,; : alicui de aliquā re,: alicui re per aliquid,.—Impers.: ut non multum Graecis cederetur,; . —
To comply with the wishes, to yield to one: cessit auctoritati amplissimi viri vel potius paruit,; cf. : precibus,: cessit tibi blandienti Cerberus,; cf,; ; ; ; ; ; 9, 16: omnes in unum cedebant,; ; cf. and 41.—Hence,
Act.: cedere (alicui) aliquid = concedere, to grant, concede, allow, give up, yield, permit something to some one: permitto aliquid iracundiae tuae, do adulescentiae, cedo amicitiae, tribuo parenti,: multa multis de jure suo,: currum ei,: victoriam hosti,: alicui pellicem et regnum,: imperium,: possessionem,: in dando et cedendo loco,.—Also with a clause as object, (but in , read credit).—And with ut and subj.: hac victoriā contenta plebes cessit patribus, ut in praesentiā tribuni crearentur, etc.,; : non cedere with quominus, .—
In respect to the terminus ad quem, to arrive, attain to, come somewhere: cedunt, petunt,: ibi ad postremum cedit miles, aes petit,.—
Trop.: hoc cedere ad factum volo,come to its execution,.—
Cedere alicui or in aliquem, to come to, fall (as a possession) to one, to fall to his lot or share,

accrue: ut is quaestus huic cederet,: captiva corpora Romanis cessere,: nolle ominari quae captae urbi cessura forent,; ; ; ; 12, 183; ; ; : undae cesserunt piscibus habitandae, al.: alicui in usum,: Lepidi atque Antonii arma in Augustum cessere,; so ; ; : aurum ex hostibus captum in paucorum praedam cessisse,; ; ; for which: cedere praedae (dat.) alicujus, ; and: praeda cedit alicui,: ab Tullo res omnis Albana in Romanum cesserit imperium,; : in dicionem M. Antonii provinciae cesserant,.—

Cedere in aliquid, like abire in aliquid (v. abeo, II.), to be changed or to pass into something, to be equivalent to or become something: poena in vicem fidei cesserat,; cf.: temeritas in gloriam cesserat,; ; ; ; : in proverbium,: in exemplorum locum,.—Hence, * cēdenter, adv. of the part. pres. cedens (not used as P. a.), by yielding, .

la:noun:certamen.html:
certāmen, ĭnis, n.
id.
,
a contest, struggle, strife, whether friendly or hostile, physical or intellectual; most freq. of a pugilistic contest of any kind; but also of contention in war.
A contest, struggle in games or otherwise.
Lit.: videmusne apud quos eorum ludorum, qui gymnici nominantur, magnus honos sit, nullum ab iis, qui in id certamen descendant, devitari dolorem?; cf. : Hac celebrata tenus sancto certamina patri,; cf. : luctandi,: saliendi,: citharoedorum,: sacra, Spald.: quinquennale triplex, musicum, gymnicum, equestre,; cf. ; : bijugum,: quadrigarum,: pedum,: cursus,; 10, 560: disci,: Veneris, et saep.—
Meton., poet., the object contended for, the prize, : pecoris magistris Velocis jaculi certamina ponit in ulmo, Heyne.—
Trop., a rivalry, contest, struggle, emulation, etc.: certamen honestum (Stoicorum et Peripateticorum),: est mihi tecum pro aris et focis certamen,: est alicui certamen cum aliquo de principatu,: certamen honoris et gloriae. ; cf. ; ; : bona ratio cum perditā confligit. In ejus modi certamine ac proelio,: pugna forensium certaminum,: eloquentiae inter juvenes,: verborum linguaeque,: laboris ac periculi,: amicitiae, benevolentiae,: bonae artis ac virtutis,: irarum,; cf. : conferendi (pecuniam),: patrum animos certamen regni ac cupido versabat,; cf. : leti (inter mulieres Indas),diu magnum inter mortales certamen fuit, vine corporis an virtute animi, etc.,; cf. .—Rarely with gen. of adversary: si in virtutis certamen venerint ( = cum virtute), Madv. ad loc.—Poet.: mite vini,a drinking bout,.—Also poet.: certamina ponere, syn. with certamina instituere = ἀγῶνα προτιθέναι, to order, arrange a fight or contest, ; ; cf. Wagn.—Of inanimate things: Arboribusque datumst variis exinde per auras Crescendi magnum inmissis certamen habenis,.—
Esp., a military strife, battle, engagement, contest, fight, combat.
Subject. (diff. from the objective; cf.: proeliam, pugna, bellum, etc.): horrida Romuleum certamina pango duellum,; ; ; 5, 1295; Planc. ap. ; ; ; : aeterno certamine proelia pugnasque edere,: fit proelium acri certamine,; cf.: proelii certamen,: certamine,with zeal, emulously, earnestly,; Curt.

9, 4; ; cf.: nec magni certaminis ea dimicatio fuit,not severe,. —

Object., = proelium, pugna, etc.: vario certamine pugnatum est,: erat in celeritate omne positum certamen, utri, etc.,: bella atque certamina,: ubi res ad certamen venit,: in certamine ipso,: navalia,a naval engagement, sea-fight,: classicum,: saevit medio in certamine Mavors, et saep.—Hence.
In the postAug. histt. for war in gen., ; ; ; .

la:noun:cena.html:
cēna (not coena, caena; old form caesna; cf.
Casmena for Camena, Müll.), ae, f.
Sanscr. khad-, eat; Umbr. çes-na; cf. Gr. κνίζω
, the principal meal of the Romans in the early period, taken about midday, dinner, supper (Paul. ex ; and 368, 8 Müll.); subsequently, the prandium was taken at noon, and the cena was usually begun about the 9th hour, i. e. at 3 o'clock P. M. (v. Dict. of Antiq. s. v. coena; cf.: prandium, jentaculum): cena apud antiquos dicebatur quod nunc est prandium. Vesperna, quam nunc cenam appellamus, Paul. ex Fest. l. l.; ; ; ; to begin sooner was an indication of gluttony,.
With substt.: cenarum ars,: caput cenae,; cf.: mullus cenae caput,: ejus cenae fundus et fundamentum omne erat aula una lentis Aegyptiae,: genus cenae sollemne, viaticum, adventicium, geniale, Philarg. ad : honos cenae,: inpensae cenarum,: cenarum magister,: ordo cenae,: cenae pater,: o noctes cenaeque deūm!: mero Pontificum potiore cenis,: Thyestae,.—
With adjj.: abundantissima,: aditialis,; : sumptuosa,: adventicia,: quorum omnis vigilandi labor in antelucanis cenis expromitur,i. e. lasting all night,: auguralis,: amplior,: bona atque magna,: brevis,: Cerialis,: dubia,; : ebria,: grandes,: lautissima,: libera,open table,: multa de magnā fercula cenā,: munda,: cena non minus nitida quam frugi,: sororia, nuptialis. :

: opimae,: popularem quam vocant,: prior,i. e. a previous invitation,: publicae,: recta,; ; : Saliares,: sollemnes,: subita,; : terrestris,of vegetables,: varia,: viatica,.—

With verbs: quid ego istius prandia, cenas commemorem?; : cenam apparare,: curare,: coquere,; ; ; ; ; : cenas facere,; cf. : anteponere,: committere maturo ovo, Varr. ap. : praebere ternis ferculis,: ducere,to prolong,: ministrare,: producere,: apponere,; : deesse cenae,: instruere pomis et oleribus,: cenam dare alicui,; ; : cenae adhibere aliquem,; ; ; ; ; ; : Taurus accipiebat nos Athenis cenā,: cenam cenavi tuam,: obire cenas,: cenam condicere alicui, to engage one's self to any one as a guest, promise to be one's guest, .—
With prepp.: ante cenam,; : inter cenam,at table,; id. Fragm. ap. ; ; ; ; ; in this sense in Suet. several times: super cenam,; ; ; ; ; ; : post cenam,.—(ε) With substt. and prepp.: aliquem Abduxi ad cenam,; : aliquem ad cenam aliquo condicam foras,; : holera et pisciculos ferre in cenam seni,: fit aliquid in cenam,is preparing,: ire ad cenam,: venire ad cenam,; : itare ad cenas,: invitare ad cenam,; ; : venire ad cenam,: promittere ad cenam,: vocare ad cenam,; ; : devocare,: redire a cenā,. —Prov.: cenā comesā venire, i. e. to come too late: post festum,: cenam rapere de rogo,of unscrupulous greed,.—
Meton.
A dish, course, at dinner: prima, altera, tertia, and 6.—*
A company at table: ingens cena sedet,.—*
The place of an entertainment (cf. cenatio and cenaculum), .

cētĕrōqui or -quīn
ceterus-qui
(like alioqui and alioquin; v. alioqui, and cf. Hand, Turs. I. p. 235), adv.,
for the rest, in other respects, otherwise, = ἄλλως (rare): quem, nisi quod solum, ceteroquin recte quidam vocant Atticum,: ego ceteroqui animo aequo fero; unum vereor, ne hasta Caesaris refrixerit,; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; cf. Hand, Turs. II. pp. 44 and 42.

la:verb:cerno.html:
cerno, crēvi, crētum (
part. pass. cretus is apparently used only once: cineris bene creti,; but freq. in the compounds of cerno; for the simple part., the orig. form certus also is very rarely used: certā deinde sorte senatus consultum factum est,; v. under II. C., and cf. certus), 3, v. a.
root car- for scar-, to separate; cf. κρίνω; hence, σκώρ, stercus, screo; cf. cera
.
To separate, sift (rare): per cribrum, Cato. R. R. 107, 1: farinam cribro,; cf. ; ; : in cribris omnia cerne cavis,; cf.: per densa foramina,: cineris bene creti,well sifted,.—Far more freq.,
Trop.
To separate, distinguish by the senses, mostly by the eyes, i. e. to perceive, see, discern (syn.: video, conspicio; class. in prose and poetry; most freq. probably in Lucretius, where it is used about a hundred times); rarely by the ears; v.infra: lumen jubarve in caelo cerno?

Enn. ap. Müll.; 7, § 76 ib.: sed quis illic est, procul quem video? estne hic Hegio? si satis cerno, is hercle'st,: tum porro varios rerum sentimus odores, nec tamen ad nareis venienteis cernimus umquam: nec voces cernere suemus,; : quod nequeunt oculis rerum primordia cerni,; v. also ; ; cf. : acute,; cf.: cerno acutum,: altaria exhalare vapore,; —Hence, sometimes opp. to hearing: ut non solum auribus acciperetur, sed etiam oculis cerneretur,; or to mental perception: quem ego tam video animo, quam ea, quae oculis cernimus,: nos enim ne nunc quidem oculis cernimus ea, quae videmus,: quae cernere et videre non possumus,; cf. : ego Catuli Cumanum ex hoc loco cerno, Pompeianum non cerno,: ut ea cernimus quae videmus,: omnia sic aperiam, ut ea cernere oculis videamini,: coram aliquid,to witness,; : aliquem,: acies a nostris cernebatur,: in sole sidera ipsa desinunt cerni,: simile quiddam facientes aves cernimus,: me miserum, turbā quod non ego cernar in illā,: Constitit alma Venus, nulli cernenda,; ; .—With acc. and inf.: sensumque inesse et motum in membris cerno, Canius ap. Müll.: neque mutari ac misceri omnia cerneres,: quos ad resistendum concucurrisse cernebat, * : cernis ut insultent Rutuli?: cerne quam tenui vos parte contingat,: cerneres, quanta audacia fuisset, etc.,.—Impers. with acc. and inf.: cernebatur, novissimos illorum premi vehementer, Herz. N. cr.— So impers. with rel. -clause: ut non solum auribus acciperetur, sed etiam oculis cerneretur quem detulisset,. —Ante-class., of the hearing: vox illius certe est: idem omnes cernimus, Att. ap. , and perh. also, Titin. ap. P.—Hence,

Cerni aliquā re or in aliquā re, to become distinguished or known in something: fortis animus et magnus duabus rebus maxime cernitur,; so : amicus certus in re incertā cernitur, Enn. ap. : atque hae quidem virtutes cernuntur in agendo,; (also in ).—*
Have before the mind, have respect to, regard any one: ubi gratus, si non eum ipsi cernunt grati, cui referunt gratiam?.—
Transf. to intellectual objects, to perceive, comprehend, understand (syn.: intellego, cognosco, perspicio): neque tanta in rebus obscuritas, ut eas (res) non penitus acri vir ingenio cernat, si modo aspexerit,: jam cernam mene an illam potiorem putes, id. poët. Tusc. 2, 9, 20: (antiquitas) hoc melius ea fortasse, quae erant vera, cernebat,; ; ; ; : quae cum ego non solum suspicarer, sed plane cernerem,; : ut consuetum facile amorem cerneres,.—Hence,
Rarely of future events, to foresee, discern beforehand: cerno animo sepultā in patriā miseros atque insepultos acervos civium,: cerno jam animo, quanto omnia uberiora atque ornatiora futura sint,.—
To decide something that is contested or doubtful (judicially), to decree, determine (more rare than decernere): quotcumque senatus creverit populusque jusserit tot sunto,: quodcumque senatus creverit agunto,, § 6: jurati cernant. Pac. ap. : illum locum tempusque consilio destinatum quid de Armeniā cernerent,: priusquam id sors cerneret,: certā sorte,after the lot was decided,.—Hence,
To decide by contending or fighting (more rare than the freq. certare, and even in Seneca's time out of use; cf. ): ferro non auro vitam (acc. respect = de vitā) cernamus utrique, Enn. ap. ; id. ap. , and ap. Müll.; Pac. ap. : nisi esset qui armis secum vellet cernere, Att. ap. : cernere ferro, (also ap. ); so, cernere certamen,; ; : pro patriā, pro liberis, pro aris atque focis suis, * Kritz N. cr. (al. certare): seu libeat duplicem sejunctim cernere martem,.—Humorously, .—
In gen., to decide for something, to conclude upon, resolve (syn.: constituo, decerno; also rare): praesidium castris educere, Lucil. ap. : acribus inter se cum armis confligere, p. 261, 6: te mihi amicam esse crevi, (crevi valet constitui, Müll.); .—Hence,
In judic. lang. t. t., of inheritances.
To resolve to enter upon an inheritance, Müll.; cf. Tit. 22, 27, and cretio.—
To make known this determination, Tit. 22, 28 and 30; .—
= adire, to enter upon an inheritance, ; ; ; ; ; .—
Trop.: debet etiam fratris Appii amorem erga me cum reliquā hereditate crevisse,; so ; , ext. 3.—P. a. v. certus.

cĕler, ĕris, e (
masc.cĕleris, Cato ap. P.; fem. celer, Liv. Andron. ap. Prisc. l. l.; cf. acer; sup. celerissimus, Enn. and Manlius ap. Prisc. l. l.) [cello; cf. Doed. la:verb:certo.html:
certo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. freq. a.
cerno
,
to decide something by a contest (cf. cerno, II. C. b.); hence, to fight, struggle, contend, combat, implying great exertion, and usually a measuring of strength (class. in prose and poetry; most freq. in a trop. signif.; syn.: decerto, contendo).
Of a physical contest of strength; mostly of battle: utrum igitur utilius Fabricio... armis cum hoste certare, an venenis?: adulescentium greges Lacedaemone videmus ipsi incredibili contentione certantis pugnis, calcibus, unguibus, morsu denique,: manu, Dietsch: proelio,: cum Gallis pro salute,; cf. : de ambiguo agro bello,: de imperio cum populo Romano,: de principatu armis,; cf. : odiis etiam prope majoribus certarunt quam viribus,: acie, et saep.—Impers.: dignus quicum certetur, Pac. ap. : certatur limine in ipso Ausoniae, ; : die quo Bedriaci certabatur,: quā in parte rex pugnae affuit, ibi aliquamdiu certatum,: in cujus (amnis) transgressu multum certato pervicit Vardanes,; .—Mostly poet. in pass.: certata lite deorum Ambracia (for the possession of which Apollo. Diana, and Hercules contended),: certatus nobis orbis (i. e. de quo certavimus),; cf. II. infra.—
Out of the sphere of milit. operations, to contend, struggle, strive, emulate, vie with: certabant urbem Romam Remoramne vocarent, Enn. ap. (Ann. v. 85 Vahl.): haut doctis dictis certantes sed maledictis, Enn. ap. (Ann. v. 274 ib.): minis mecum, minaciis,: malitiā tecum,: benedictis,: certare ingenio, contendere nobilitate,: cum aliquo dicacitate,: officiis inter se,; cf.: certatum inter collegas maledictis,; and: eo modo inter se duo imperatores certabant,: cum civibus de virtute,: pro sua quisque potentia,: contumaciā adversus contemnentes humilitatem suam nobiles certavit (Licinius),: cum usuris fructibus praediorum, to contend against interest (to strive to pay interest) with the produce of estates, : cum a Cheruscis Longobardisque pro antiquo decore aut recenti libertate; et contra, augendae dominationi certaretur,: ob hircum,: joco,: mero,: animis iniquis,: parsimoniā et vigiliis et labore cum ultimis militum,: sententiis,: ut si nautae certarent, quis eorum potissimum gubernaret,: mos gentis est, equitare jaculari cursu cum aequalibus certare,: dic mecum quo pignore certes,: celeri sagittā,: certemus, spinas animone ego fortius an tu Evellas agro,.— Poet., with acc.: hanc rem ( = de hac re), Sedigit. ap. ; cf. in pass.: cui (multae) certandae cum dies advenisset,.—With dat. instead of cum: solus tibi certat Amyntas,; ; ; ; ; ; ; .—
Particularly of judicial disputations, to contend at law: inter se,; cf. , § 32: in centumvirali judicio,: si a duumviris provocarit, provocatione certato,: si quid se judice certes,: foro si res certabitur olim,.—
With inf. (mostly poet.), to strive to do something, to labor, endeavor, struggle earnestly, to exert one's self: certantes ad summum succedere honorem,; so, inter se cernere,: dimittere se (nubes),: populum alium suorum sepelire,: Phoebum superare canendo,: superare,: vincere,: tollere (hunc) tergeminis honoribus,: inter se eruere quercum,: certat quisque evadere,: frangere fluctus,; ; .

la:verb:cesso.html:
cesso, āvi, ātum, 1,
v. freq. n. and a. [1. cedo]; lit., to stand back very much; hence, to be remiss in any thing, to delay, loiter, or, in gen., to cease from, stop, give over (indicating a blamable remissness; while desinere, intermittere, requiescere do not include that idea: cessat desidiosus, requiescit fessus, Don. ad . Diff. from cunctari in this, that the latter designates inaction arising from want of resolution, but cessare that which is the result of slothfulness; cf. Doed. Syn. 3, p. 300 sq.; class. in prose and poetry): paulum si cessassem,; ; : si tabellarii non cessarint,: in suo studio atque opere,: ne quis in eo, quod me viderit facientem, cesset,; cf. : ab apparatu operum ac munitionum nihil cessatum,; ; ; : quidquid apud durae cessatum est moenia Trojae,whatever delay there was,: audaciā,to be deficient in spirit,; cf.: nullo umquam officio,: ad arma cessantes Concitet, et saep.—So in admonitions: quid cessas?; : quid cessatis?: quor cessas?; cf.: cessas in vota precesque (poet. for cessas facere vota), Tros, ait, Aenea? cessas? ; .— With dat. incommodi: it dies; ego mihi cesso,i. e. to my own injury, Lorenz ad loc.; : sed ego nunc mihi cesso, qui non umerum hunc onero pallio,.—
With inf.: ego hinc migrare cesso,: numquid principio cessavit verbum docte dicere?; so, alloqui,; : adoriri,: pultare ostium,; : introrumpere,: detrahere de nobis,: mori, et saep.—
In gen.
To be inactive, idle, at leisure, to do nothing: cur tam multos deos nihil agere et cessare patitur? cur non rebus humanis aliquos otiosos deos praeficit?; cf. ; : nisi forte ego vobis cessare nunc videor; cum bella non gero,: et si quid cessare potes, requiesce sub umbrā,: cessabimus una, : cur alter fratrum cessare et ludere et ungi praeferat, etc., (cessare otiari et jucunde vivere, Schol. Crucq.); so : per hibernorum tempus,: cessatum usque adhuc est: nunc porro expergiscere,: cessatum ducere curam,put to rest,: non timido, non ignavo cessare tum licuit,.—
Of things, to be at rest, to rest, be still, inactive, unemployed, or unused, etc.: si cessare putas rerum primordia posse, Cessandoque novos rerum progignere motus,: quid ita cessarunt pedes?: et grave suspenso vomere cesset opus,; : Achilles cessare in Teucros pertulit arma sua,: cur Berecyntiae Cessant flamina tibiae,: cessat voluntas?: cessat ira deae,: solas sine ture relictas Praeteritae cessasse ferunt Letoïdos aras,i. e. remained unsought, unapproached,; cf.: at nunc desertis cessant sacraria lucis, and: cessaturae casae,: cessans honor,a vacant office,.—
Of land, to lie uncultivated, fallow (cf. cessatio): alternis idem tonsas cessare novales,; ; cf. .—Pass.: cessata arva,.—Trop., of a barren woman, .—
Sometimes cessare alicui rei, like vacare alicui rei, to have leisure for something, i.e. to attend to, apply one's self to: amori,.—
Rarely (prob. not ante-Aug.), not to be at hand or present, to be wanting: cessat voluntas? non aliā bibam Mercede,: augendum addendumque quod cessat,.—Hence,
Judic. t. t.
Of persons, not to appear before a tribunal, to make default: culpāne quis an aliquā necessitate cessasset, (where,

just before, absentibus; cf. absum, 8.): quoties delator adesse jussus cessat,; so .—

Of things (a process, verdict), to be invalid, null, void: cessat injuriarum actio,: revocatio,: edictum,: senatus consultum, et saep.—
Also rare, in a moral view, to depart from a right way, i.e. to mistake, err: ut scriptor si peccat... Sic qui multum cessat,: oratoris perfecti illius, ex nullā parte cessantis,.

senses: tell me!; describe (it) to me!, explain (it) to me!
la:verb:cedo#2.html:
cēdo, cessi, cessum, 3, v. n. and a.
[perh. for cecado, redupl. from cado], to go, i. e. to be in motion, move, walk, go along.
In gen.
Lit. (rare, and only poet.: for which, in the common lang., incedo); candidatus cedit hic mastigia,: non prorsus, verum transvorsus cedit, quasi cancer,; cf. ; .—More freq.,
Trop.
Like ire, to have some result, to eventuate, happen, result, turn out, to work; and, acc. to its connection, to turn out well or ill, to succeed or fail: gesta quae prospere ei cesserunt,; ; : cetera secundum eventum proelii cessura,; ; : bene,; ; : optime,: male,; and: male alicui,; ; cf. ; : utcumque cesserit,; cf. ; : parum,: opinione tardius,: pro bono,: in vanum (labor),. —
Cedere pro aliquā re, to be equivalent to, to go for something, to be the price of: oves, quae non peperint, binae pro singulis in fructu cedent,; ; ; .—
In partic.
In respect to the terminus a quo.
To go from somewhere, to remove, withdraw, go away from, depart, retire (freq. and class.): cedunt de caelo corpora avium, Vahl.: quia postremus cedis,: ego cedam atque abibo,: cedens carinā,; cf. : quoquam,: aliquo sucus de corpore cessit,: coma de vertice,: e toto corpore anima,: ex ingratā civitate,: e patriā,: patriā,: Italiā,; ; —
Milit. t. t.: de oppidis,to abandon, go away from,: loco,to yield, give up his post,; ; ; et saep.: ex loco,: ex acie,.—
In commercial lang. t. t.: foro, to withdraw from themarket, i. e. to give up business, be insolvent, stop payment, ; ; .—So also,
Bonis or possessionibus (alicui), to give up or cede one's property or interest (in favor of a person): alicui hortorum possessione,; so ; cf. ; ; ; .— Hence of debtors, to make over their property instead of payment; cf. , tit. de cessione bonorum.—
Pregn. (cf. abeo, II.), to pass away, disappear; and specif.,
Of men, to die: vitā,; : e vita,; ; cf. senatu,to withdraw from,; .—
Of time, to pass away, vanish: horae quidem cedunt et dies et menses et anni,. —
Of other things: pudor ex pectore cessit, Lucil. ap. : memoriā, (for which: excedere memoriā,; and: excedere e memoriā,): non Turno fiducia cessit,: cedant curaeque metusque, et saep.; cf. cesso.—
Trop.: cedere alicui or absol., to yield to one (to his superiority), to give the preference or precedence, give place to, submit to (class.; esp. freq. in the histt., of the weaker party, withdrawing, fleeing from).
To yield to, give place to: quācumque movemur, (aër) videtur quasi locum dare et cedere,: cedebat victa potestas,: ubi vinci necesse est, expedit cedere,; ; ; cf. : Viriatho exercitus nostri imperatoresque cesserunt,; ; ; ; ; ; et saep.: Pelides cedere nescius,: di, quibus ensis et ignis Cesserunt,i. e. who remained unhurt in the destruction of Troy,: eidem tempori, ejusdem furori, eisdem consulibus, eisdem minis, insidiis, periculis,; so, fortunae,: invidiae ingratorum civium,: majorum natu auctoritati,: nocti,, and 3, 60, 7; 4, 55, 5; cf. : loco iniquo, non hosti cessum,: oneri,: vincentibus vitiis,: malis, et saep.—
To yield to in rank, distinction, etc., i. e. to be inferior to: cum tibi aetas nostra jam cederet, fascesque summitteret,: nullā aliā re nisi immortalitate cedens caelestibus,: neque multum cedebant virtute nostris,; : Picenis cedunt pomis Tiburtia suco; Nam facie praestant,; so, anseribus (candore),: laudibus lanificae artis,; 5, 529: cum in re nullā Agesilao cederet,; : alicui de aliquā re,: alicui re per aliquid,.—Impers.: ut non multum Graecis cederetur,; . —
To comply with the wishes, to yield to one: cessit auctoritati amplissimi viri vel potius paruit,; cf. : precibus,: cessit tibi blandienti Cerberus,; cf,; ; ; ; ; ; 9, 16: omnes in unum cedebant,; ; cf. and 41.—Hence,
Act.: cedere (alicui) aliquid = concedere, to grant, concede, allow, give up, yield, permit something to some one: permitto aliquid iracundiae tuae, do adulescentiae, cedo amicitiae, tribuo parenti,: multa multis de jure suo,: currum ei,: victoriam hosti,: alicui pellicem et regnum,: imperium,: possessionem,: in dando et cedendo loco,.—Also with a clause as object, (but in , read credit).—And with ut and subj.: hac victoriā contenta plebes cessit patribus, ut in praesentiā tribuni crearentur, etc.,; : non cedere with quominus, .—
In respect to the terminus ad quem, to arrive, attain to, come somewhere: cedunt, petunt,: ibi ad postremum cedit miles, aes petit,.—
Trop.: hoc cedere ad factum volo,come to its execution,.—
Cedere alicui or in aliquem, to come to, fall (as a possession) to one, to fall to his lot or share,

accrue: ut is quaestus huic cederet,: captiva corpora Romanis cessere,: nolle ominari quae captae urbi cessura forent,; ; ; ; 12, 183; ; ; : undae cesserunt piscibus habitandae, al.: alicui in usum,: Lepidi atque Antonii arma in Augustum cessere,; so ; ; : aurum ex hostibus captum in paucorum praedam cessisse,; ; ; for which: cedere praedae (dat.) alicujus, ; and: praeda cedit alicui,: ab Tullo res omnis Albana in Romanum cesserit imperium,; : in dicionem M. Antonii provinciae cesserant,.—

Cedere in aliquid, like abire in aliquid (v. abeo, II.), to be changed or to pass into something, to be equivalent to or become something: poena in vicem fidei cesserat,; cf.: temeritas in gloriam cesserat,; ; ; ; : in proverbium,: in exemplorum locum,.—Hence, * cēdenter, adv. of the part. pres. cedens (not used as P. a.), by yielding, .

la:noun:ce.html:
-cĕ, an inseparable strengthening demonstrative particle, answering etymol. to the Gr. γέ (Sanscr. ki; cf. Lat. ci-s and citra), and in signif. to the demonstr. ι (in οὑτοσί, τουτί, etc.), appended to words in different forms.
Unchanged ce: hicce, haecce, hocce; also in MSS. and inscriptions one c: hice, etc.; plur.: hice, haece, haecce; gen. hujusce, etc.—
Changed,
Into ci before the interrog. particle ne: hiccine, hoccine, siccine, nunccine, etc. (v. hic, sic, nunc, etc.).—
By a rejection of e, in hic, haec, hoc, nunc, etc. for hice, haece, hoce, nunce, etc.; illic, istic, nunc, sic (for illice, etc.); cf. Zumpt, Gram. § 132; Corss. Ausspr II. p. 235.
